Most trends follow the same arc:

A: Mania                                                         B: Hate
_____________|______________________________________
              Vibe coding
              Claude infographics
              AI copywriting

Once something hits the mania extreme, it starts its journey to the hate zone – because people overuse the same tactic again and again.

My main timeline on X is something I rarely visit now – I'm fucking tired of “My Claude guide to earn 5,000 bucks per hour” and “Best skills for your Claude agent.”

Everybody's shipping tools. Everybody's trying to sell their services. Everybody's building their founder personas.

Same faces, same hooks, same design decisions – again and again.

The supply is so huge, it's almost impossible to decide what you actually need.

Imo, we're approaching a time of critical consumer inertia, where people don't want to try new things.

Because “new things” are the same grey mass.

I'd love to end with a motivational tip, but I don't know how to break this barrier yet.

A lot of what I'm building lands in that same “grey mass” zone – especially for people who don't know me and don't have those extra 3 seconds to give me to prove value.

So maybe close circle is the real answer?

thread_tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
A recent example: @imakhercha sends me a 2022 paper by Bennett, Cucuringu & Reinert on lead-lag detection.

Lead-lag is old MFT territory (Huth & Abergel, 2011). What hooks him is the antisymmetric part of the second-order path signature: a signed-area measure that captures the order in which signals move.

He adapts it to order flow and book imbalance, builds a PoC in 2 hours (that part is absolutely crazy to me), tests it, then gets the bot running on a $5k account with our basic risk layer.

A few days later: 4.1 Sharpe and +14% return, net of fees.

To state the obvious it's not (yet) something we could put in prod, because of capacity and risk, and we already have the whole infra around and the best fee tiers, but it just tells you at which pace trading firms are able to move today, and how much you could parallelize alpha research if you have the infra to do it.

I think the complaints of people who are unhappy about EIP-8037 breaking a few contracts are valid and very reasonable.

We do NOT want an Ethereum where it becomes "prudent security advice" to have centralized upgrade hatches "just in case".

I do think that on-net 8037, and a couple of other large breaking changes coming up, are necessary to get Ethereum to a healthy long-term stable state. But it should not be *easy* to make such deep changes to Ethereum. A social norm that, at the very least, core devs have a responsibility to support any app that breaks because a fork broke some aspect of Ethereum that the devs justifiably thought was rock solid is very good to have.

To that end I'm glad that people in @ethereumfndn, @ethlabs_org and elsewhere have been working hard to help app devs with upgrades. Such efforts should continue and increase. Given its breaking nature, Glamsterdam should not be rushed.

I also hope everyone on all sides stays engaged for similar conversations around the next few forks.

Some of my thoughts on the trend of protocols launching on @Enter_Elysium rn, drawing parallels to what I observed on early days RH chain:

Phase 1: launchpad war / Meme era

Elys started off with mostly launchpad and memes (Ascend, Montra, Eaac, Eaccat, Blob etc) not much value buying here other than trying to potentially position for the winning pad + greatest mindshare meme

Phase 2: Cool tech bro

then follows the actual “cool tech” phase, where teams building here are focused on solving some unique problem in its own kind (this is where I think we are rn) and imo this is one of the easier phases to capitalize on; as it’s easier to sieve through the tech and problem statement each protocol is solving vs trying to see which meme has more social capital for i.e

Phase 3: Slop tech

As price of the cool tech protocols float up, the next wave that naturally follows will be “slop-tech”, where extractors come to find a home for easy capital to fomo and chase the cool tech betas. This is where you’ll find a slop version of a cool tech protocol built in 2 days but tweaked v1.1 to add some feature and spin it off as its own. 

Since slop tech founders dgaf about building long term, they can’t or won’t innovate past v1.1, unlike the cool tech protocols teams could, naturally value wouldn’t accrue there over time past the hype phase

Phase 4: Capital inflow slowdown

Capital inflow eventually slows down to Elys chain esp if everyone who wants to be allocated has allocated. Arrival of slop tech means that any one late to Elys would be chasing these beta plays over the incumbent in hope for larger gains. But because these slop tech founders aren’t here because they want to for the tech but mainly capital flows to feast on easy rotational capital, safe to assume that capital will be rolled off via Elys to their bank accounts 

Phase 5: Consolidation of capital

Large pullbacks across the entire eco happens as the last buyer has bought, and no net inflow is happening at current valuations. A general consolidation / pullback to where “fair value” exists for all projects and this means 70-80+% drawdowns. Slop tech goes to 0, cool tech continues to build and chart establishes a range. 

Eventually the consolidation reaches an apex and a fundamental trigger reignited the capital inflow back into the chain and we go back to phase 2, where capital first reallocated to the cool tech and the cycle repeats

I think we are in phase 2 rn for Elysium

Leopold's Situational Awareness Q3 Letter is excellent but long (167 pages) so I made a recap video! Overall I very much agree with most predictions made. (link to the letter at the end)

Most important predictions I read:
• 3 years of AI progress in 2027. The median estimate is 3.0x, with a range of 1.8–6.2x. That is a jump as big as GPT-4 (high schooler) to Opus 5.5 (summer associate or L5 engineer), on top of today's models by the end of 2027.
• Progress keeps speeding up. AI already runs about 1.9x a normal year's pace and reaches roughly 5.2x by the end of 2027 (16.6x in the bull case), because models are starting to automate AI research.
• "Virtual departments" replace "virtual interns." Hundreds of agents work persistently for weeks under their own managers. He expects these multi-agent systems "will be to 2027 as agents were to 2026."
• $1T+ in combined lab revenue run rate by the end of 2027, with anything from $500B to multiple trillions plausible. Wall Street's $150–200B for Anthropic would require AI to stagnate.
• Anthropic could be the most profitable company in the world by the end of 2027, passing Aramco, Nvidia and Samsung.
• AI compute gets far more valuable. An H100 earned $1–2/hour, earns $5–10/hour today, and goes to "$100s/hour+" as AI nears superintelligence.
• The market is the one making the radical forecast. It prices a 0.3–0.6x progress year: memory makers at one times next year's earnings and datacenters at only the contracts already signed.
• The real risk is political, not technical. A terrible accident could trigger a crackdown, but most paths still mean progress "far faster than the market expects."
• A ChatGPT moment for robotics is starting, with a buildout to billions of robots.
• Over $500T of wealth created and about $500T destroyed. Most companies lose most of their value as superintelligence makes their employees, IP and management obsolete. That includes many of today's AI winners and perhaps 400+ of the S&P 500.

Full letter: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1EGizl1XHseWsv_ZyBWd-Z-VVpdITceEF/view?usp=sharing
